storyBeat: Ana meets Emir at the Sebilj fountain and learns to introduce herself.

grammar.title: biti. Sam, si, je
grammar.explanation: The verb biti means to be. Beginners live on three short forms. Say ja sam for I am. Say ti si for you are. Say on je or ona je for he is or she is. Put the pronoun first when you want clarity, as in Ja sam Ana.

grammar.title: Two ways to introduce yourself
grammar.explanation: Ja sam Ana states identity with biti. Zovem se Ana means “I am called Ana” or “my name is Ana.” Both are natural. For “nice to meet you,” say Drago mi je, which literally means “it is dear to me.”

grammar.title: iz. Saying where you are from
grammar.explanation: Use iz plus a place for origin. Say Ja sam iz Amerike. Say Emir je iz Sarajeva.

culture.title: Sebilj. Where people meet
culture.body: The Sebilj is a wooden fountain in the middle of Baščaršija’s main square. Locals and visitors use it as a landmark: “Kod Sebilja” means meet me at the fountain. Pigeons gather, photos happen, and first hellos often start here. Emir waits for Ana at Sebilj. A classic Sarajevo rendezvous.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A. Pronouns and biti
lessonBlocks.body: Learn four pronouns in this lesson. Ja means I. Ti means you in informal speech. On means he. Ona means she. Pair them with biti. Say ja sam, ti si, on je, and ona je. Say them aloud until they feel automatic. Then build tiny truths. Say Ja sam Ana. Say Ti si Emir. Say On je vodič. Say Ona je prijateljica. We will meet more she words soon. For now Ona je Ana is enough. Beginners often drop the pronoun when the verb form is clear, but keeping Ja sam Ana is clearer and friendlier while you learn.
tips: Drill ja sam, ti si, on je, and ona je.
Keep the pronoun when you introduce yourself with Ja sam.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B. Meeting Emir
lessonBlocks.body: At Sebilj, Ana needs a meeting script. Start with a greeting from Lesson 1, such as Zdravo! Or Dobar dan! Then say Zovem se Ana. Or say Ja sam Ana. Add origin if you want with Ja sam iz Amerike. When Emir answers, reply Drago mi je! Listen for On je Emir, Ja sam Emir, or Zovem se Emir. All of those are fine. End with a smile and maybe Hvala when he offers help. Tomorrow you will drink kahva with Amira. In this lesson you only need to be Ana.
tips: Meeting order is Zdravo, then Ja sam or Zovem se, then Drago mi je.
Reuse Lesson 1 greetings. Do not invent new ones yet.

funFacts.title: Sebilj means a public fountain
funFacts.body: Sebilj started as a practical word for a public fountain kiosk. The term comes from Ottoman Turkish roots for water offered to everyone in the square. Sarajevo’s Sebilj is now a city icon and a favorite meeting point. When Emir says to meet kod Sebilja, he is using landmark language locals still rely on.

funFacts.title: sam / si / je are clitics
funFacts.body: The short biti forms sam, si, and je act like little grammar hitchhikers. In longer sentences they usually land in second position, right after the first word. Beginners do not need the full theory on day one. For now, keep your Ja sam patterns clear and let the rest come with practice.

funFacts.title: Drago mi je is warm rather than stiff
funFacts.body: Drago mi je is the standard way to say nice to meet you. It sounds warm in cafés, offices, and first introductions. Ana and Emir use it because real meetings need more than a name. Learn it as one ready phrase, then say it like you mean the welcome.

funFacts.title: Pigeons optional, rendezvous required
funFacts.body: Meeting kod Sebilja is local shorthand for a reliable rendezvous. Landmarks beat street numbers when your phone battery dies. Pigeons and photos are optional extras around the fountain. The useful skill is knowing how Bosnians point to a place everyone can find.

civicContext.title: Who is allowed to hold the highest offices
civicContext.body: Bosnia and Herzegovina’s constitution still blocks some citizens from the highest state offices because of ethnicity. Key posts such as the tripartite Presidency and seats in the House of Peoples are reserved for Bosniacs, Croats, and Serbs as constituent peoples. Jews, Roma, and other citizens outside those labels cannot hold those offices. The European Court of Human Rights ruled against that exclusion in Sejdić and Finci in 2009, and the judgment has still not been fully implemented.
